title: Hot and cold: what makes warmth, and what only keeps it in

summary.text: We call a sweater warm, but does a sweater make any warmth? Your child puts two katoris of fridge-cold coconut oil on a table, and wraps one of them in a sweater. The bare oil melts first, and the oil inside the sweater stays white and hard for longer. So a sweater makes no warmth. It only slows warmth moving in or out. The warmth you feel inside a sweater comes from your own body, which makes it from food. Your child also hunts for the things that really make warmth: the Sun, fire, electricity in an iron box, rubbing, and living bodies.
summary.art: Two small steel katoris on a kitchen table, one wrapped in a folded red sweater and one bare with clear runny oil, and a girl peeping into the sweater to see white hard oil.

intro.hook: Hold a sweater, a shawl or a blanket against your cheek. Is it warm?
intro.text: Most people say yes, because we call these warm clothes. But a sweater lying on a chair feels only as warm as the chair. Put it on, and in a minute or two it feels warm. So where did that warmth come from? In this unit you find out which things make warmth and which only keep it in.
intro.art: A child holding a folded sweater against one cheek with a puzzled face, and the same sweater lying on a chair behind them.

outcomes: By the end I can say whether things are hot, warm, cool or cold, and that temperature is how hot or cold something is.
By the end I can name things that make warmth: the Sun, fire, electricity in an iron or a kettle, rubbing, and living bodies.
By the end I can say that a sweater or a blanket makes no warmth, and only slows warmth moving in or out.
By the end I can explain that my body makes its own warmth from food, all day and all night.
By the end I can do a fair test with two katoris of cold coconut oil, and say what I saw.
By the end I can say that hot things cool down and cold things warm up, until they are as warm as the room.
By the end I can name ways that people and other animals keep warm and cool down.

terms.meaning: Hot and cold are words for how much warmth a thing has. Hot things have a lot of warmth. Cold things have little.
terms.example: An idli straight from the steamer is hot. An ice cube is cold.
terms.art: A steaming idli on a banana leaf next to an ice cube on a steel plate.

terms.meaning: Warm is a little hot. Cool is a little cold.
terms.example: A bath can be warm. Water from a clay matka is cool.
terms.art: A bucket of bath water with a little steam, next to a clay pot with a tumbler of water beside it.

terms.meaning: Temperature is how hot or cold something is. A thermometer measures it.
terms.example: On a summer afternoon in Chennai, the air has a high temperature. On a winter morning in Ooty, it has a low one.
terms.art: A sunny city street on one side and a frosty hill garden on the other.

terms.meaning: Heat is warmth on the move, from a hotter thing to a cooler thing.
terms.example: When you hold a cup of hot milk, heat moves from the milk into your hands.
terms.art: Two small hands around a steel tumbler of hot milk, with soft orange arrows going from the cup into the hands.

terms.meaning: Body heat is the warmth a living body makes from food, all the time.
terms.example: A dog curled up asleep on a mat is warm, because their body makes warmth.
terms.art: A brown dog curled up asleep on a cotton mat, with soft warm colours around them.

terms.meaning: To melt is to change from a solid into a liquid when warmed.
terms.example: Cold coconut oil is white and hard. When it warms, it melts into a clear liquid.
terms.art: A spoon of hard white coconut oil next to a spoon of clear golden oil.

terms.meaning: An insulator is a material that slows heat moving through it. Wool, cloth and feathers are insulators.
terms.example: A woollen sweater is an insulator. It slows your body heat from getting out.
terms.art: A woollen sweater with small arrows of warmth inside it, most of them turning back towards the body.

terms.meaning: To shiver is to shake without meaning to. Your muscles do it when you are cold, and it makes warmth.
terms.example: Getting out of a cold bath, you may shiver until you are dry and warm.
terms.art: A child wrapped in a towel after a bath, shoulders shaking a little, with small wavy lines around them.

explanations.definition: Temperature is how hot or cold something is.
explanations.description: Your skin can tell hot from cold. A tumbler of fridge water feels cold, and a cup of tea feels hot. Scientists use one word for how hot or cold something is: temperature. A high temperature means hot, and a low one means cold. To measure it exactly, people use a thermometer.
examples: Your forehead feels warm to the back of your hand.
A steel plate left in the sun at noon feels hot.
A tumbler of fridge water feels cold.
explanations.art: A row of five things from cold to hot: an ice cube, a matka tumbler, a hand, a cup of tea, a dosa tawa with a little smoke.

explanations.definition: Warmth is made when sunlight lands on things, when things burn, when electricity flows through an iron or a kettle, when things rub, and inside living bodies.
explanations.description: Some things make warmth. The Sun does, and its light warms what it lands on. A gas flame or a diya burns, and burning makes warmth. An iron box and a kettle turn electricity into warmth. Rubbing your hands together makes them warm. Living bodies make warmth from food all the time, yours, a dog's and a hen's.
examples: The sunny spot on the floor where a cat likes to sleep.
The flame under the dosa tawa.
Your two palms, after you rub them fast.
explanations.art: Five small pictures in a ring: the Sun, a diya flame, an iron box, two rubbing hands and a sleeping dog.

explanations.concept: A sweater keeps warmth in, but makes none
explanations.definition: A sweater, a blanket or a quilt is an insulator. It slows heat moving through it, in either direction.
explanations.description: In the Sweater and Coconut Oil test, the bare oil melted first, and the oil in the sweater stayed hard for longer. The room's warmth was moving into both katoris, and the sweater slowed it down. If the sweater made warmth, the wrapped oil would have melted first. When you wear a sweater, your body makes the warmth, and the sweater slows it from leaving you. Wool holds still air between its hairs, and still air lets heat through slowly.
examples: A quilt keeps you warm at night because it keeps your body heat in.
Chapatis wrapped in a cloth stay warm, because the cloth keeps their heat in.
An ice lolly wrapped in newspaper melts more slowly on the way home.
explanations.art: Two katoris side by side: the bare one with clear runny oil, the wrapped one opened to show white hard oil inside a folded sweater.

explanations.concept: Your body makes its own warmth
explanations.definition: Your body makes warmth from food, all day and all night. Inside, you are about 37 degrees Celsius, about as warm as a warm bath.
explanations.description: Food is your body's fuel. Your cells use it slowly, together with the air you breathe, and this gives out warmth. That is why you are warm even while you sleep. When you run or jump, your muscles work harder and make more warmth. Other animals with fur or feathers make their warmth in the same way.
examples: After running up the stairs, your cheeks feel warm.
A hen sits on her eggs, and her body keeps them warm.
Puppies sleep in a heap and keep each other warm.
explanations.art: A girl eating a plate of idli and sambar, with soft warm light glowing from inside her body.

explanations.concept: Hot things cool down, and cold things warm up
explanations.definition: Heat moves from a warmer thing to a cooler thing. In the end, both are equally warm.
explanations.description: A hot dosa left on a plate slowly gets cool. Its heat moves out into the plate and the air. A cold tumbler from the fridge slowly gets warmer. Heat from the room moves into it. Each one ends up as warm as the room. That is why the bare coconut oil melted. It had been in the cold fridge, and the warmer room was heating it.
examples: A cup of filter coffee forgotten on the table is cool an hour later.
Curd taken out of the fridge is no longer cold after a while.
An ice cube on a plate melts into a puddle of water.
explanations.art: A hot dosa with fading steam on one side and a frosty steel tumbler with drops of water on the other, both on the same table.

explanations.description: When you get cold, you start to shiver. Tiny bumps called goosebumps come up on your skin. This happens without you planning it. Your skin feels the cold, and your body acts. Your cells and nerves sense the cold and decide what to do about it. Thinking is not only something brains do.
examples: Shivering after a swim.
Goosebumps on your arms on a cold morning.
A crow fluffing up their feathers on a cold window ledge.

perspectives.who: Many scientists who study living things
perspectives.explanation: Every living cell senses what is around it and responds. A body is full of these sensing parts, working together. Shivering is the body taking care of itself.
Shivering is a reflex. Nerves send signals to a part of the brain, and it switches on shivering, like a switch on a heater. They say no one part of the body is deciding.

explanations.art: A child's arm with goosebumps, and a crow on a ledge with fluffed-up feathers, on a misty morning.

explanations.definition: We cool down when heat leaves our body faster than we make it.
explanations.description: On a hot day, your body still makes warmth. To stay comfortable, that warmth must leave you. A fan blows air past your skin, and the moving air carries warmth away. When sweat dries on your skin, it takes warmth with it. Shade keeps the Sun's light off you. A dog pants, and a cow looks for shade under a tree.
examples: Sitting under a ceiling fan in the afternoon.
A wet cloth on your forehead on a hot day.
A buffalo lying in a pond to cool off.
explanations.art: A buffalo lying in a muddy pond with only their head and back showing, and a dog panting in the shade of a tree.

agreed.text: A sweater, a blanket or a quilt makes no warmth. It slows heat moving in or out.
agreed.evidence: A thermometer wrapped in a sweater on a chair reads the same as the room. Cold things wrapped in wool stay cold for longer.

agreed.text: Humans and other animals with fur or feathers make warmth inside their bodies from food.
agreed.evidence: Measurements of breathing and body heat show that the more food a body uses, the more warmth it gives out.

agreed.text: Heat moves by itself from warmer things to cooler things.
agreed.evidence: Hot food always cools to the warmth of the room, and cold food warms up to it. No one has ever seen it go the other way by itself.

agreed.text: The inside of a healthy human body stays close to 37 degrees Celsius.
agreed.evidence: Doctors have measured the temperature of millions of people. It changes a little through the day and from person to person.

challenging.claim: A sweater or a blanket makes heat.
challenging.who: A common idea among children and grown-ups
challenging.for: When we put on a sweater, we feel warm, and we call woollens warm clothes.
challenging.against: In the coconut oil test, the oil inside the sweater stayed cold and hard longest. A sweater on a chair is as cool as the chair.
challenging.context: This card is about whether a sweater makes warmth.

challenging.claim: You lose most of your body heat through your head, so a cap matters most.
challenging.who: A common saying in many countries
challenging.for: Your head often sticks out of your clothes, so it does lose heat on a cold day.
challenging.against: Tests show the head loses about as much heat as any other bare part of the body of the same size. A bare head loses a lot only because the rest of you is covered.
challenging.context: This card is about where your body heat escapes.

challenging.claim: Being cold gives you a cold.
challenging.who: A common idea in many homes
challenging.for: Colds are more common in cool, wet weather. In one test in Britain, people who sat with their feet in cold water got cold symptoms more often in the next few days.
challenging.against: A cold is caused by tiny germs called viruses, not by cold air. Ellen Foxman, Akiko Iwasaki and their team found that one common cold virus grows better in a cool nose. So cold may help a virus, but the virus is needed.
challenging.context: This card is about whether cold weather causes colds.

challenging.claim: Some foods heat the body and some cool it, like mango and curd.
challenging.who: A common idea in many Indian homes, from Ayurveda and Siddha
challenging.for: People say they feel hot or cool after some foods. Hot chilli can make you sweat.
challenging.against: Scientists have not found that a mango or a bowl of curd changes body temperature by much. In these traditions, 'hot' and 'cold' foods may describe other effects on the body, not temperature.
challenging.context: This card is about 'heating' and 'cooling' foods.

big_questions.q: If a sweater makes no warmth, why do we call it a warm sweater?
big_questions.hint: Think about who feels warm, and where that warmth comes from.

big_questions.q: Is a sweater a warm thing or a cold thing?
big_questions.hint: Remember the coconut oil. What did the sweater do to the cold oil?

big_questions.q: When two people hug, who is warming whom?
big_questions.hint: Both bodies make warmth. Does heat move both ways, or from the warmer one?

big_questions.q: Your warmth comes from your food. Where did the food get it from?
big_questions.hint: Think about the rice plant in the sunny field.

big_questions.q: A fish in a cold river is as cold as the water. Does the fish feel cold?
big_questions.hint: Every animal lives in their own kind of warmth. What would cold mean to them?

story.title: Arjun's Cold Idli
story.note: Paati means grandmother in Tamil. Ooty, also called Udhagamandalam, is a hill town in the Nilgiris in Tamil Nadu, where winter mornings can bring frost. Meenakshi, Arjun, Paati and Rosie are made up.
text: Meenakshi was eight. She lived in Chennai, where it is warm nearly all year. In December, she and her little brother Arjun went to stay with their Paati in Ooty. Ooty is a town high up in the Nilgiri hills. Arjun was five.
On the first morning, Meenakshi woke up and gasped. The air in the room was cold. Outside the window, the grass was white with frost. Frost is tiny bits of ice that form on very cold nights.
'Sweaters on!' called Paati from the kitchen.
Meenakshi's red sweater lay folded on the chair, where it had been all night. She pulled it over her head. 'Brrr! Paati, my sweater is cold!' she said.
'Wait two minutes,' said Paati, smiling.
Meenakshi waited. Slowly, the sweater began to feel warm and soft. She frowned. On the chair it had been cold. On her it was warm. What had changed?

At breakfast, Paati gave them hot idlis with coconut chutney. Arjun ate slowly, because he was watching a big black crow on the wall. The crow had puffed up their feathers until they looked twice as fat. By the time Arjun looked back at his plate, his last idli was cold.
'I know!' said Arjun. 'Sweaters are warm.' He took off his blue sweater and wrapped his idli in it. Then he put the bundle on the chair.
Ten minutes later, he unwrapped it and took a bite. 'Still cold! This sweater is broken!'
Meenakshi laughed. Then she stopped laughing, because she remembered her own cold sweater on the chair. 'Paati,' she said, 'is a sweater warm or not?'
Paati put down her coffee. 'Feel your sweater now, on your arm,' she said. 'Where did that warmth come from?'
Meenakshi thought about it. The chair was not warm. The room was not warm. 'From me?' she said slowly.

'From you,' said Paati. 'Your body makes warmth all day and all night, from the food you eat. Your sweater makes none of its own. It only keeps your warmth close to you. So it does not escape into the cold air.'
'Then why did my idli stay cold?' asked Arjun.
'Because your idli had no warmth left to keep,' said Meenakshi. 'The sweater kept it just as cold as it was.' Paati nodded.

After breakfast, the Sun climbed over the hill. They took their tumblers of milk out to the verandah. Paati's cat, Rosie, was already lying in the one bright patch of sunlight. She had found the warmest spot in the house.

Meenakshi decided to count the things that warmed them. The Sun on the verandah was one. The gas flame under Paati's milk pan was two. Then Arjun rubbed his hands together fast, and they felt warm. That was three. He ran three times round the garden and came back pink and puffing. Running makes a body give out even more warmth. 'And our bodies,' said Meenakshi. 'That is four. And Rosie's body is five.'
'What about our sweaters?' asked Arjun.
'Sweaters do not make warmth,' said Meenakshi. 'They only keep it in.'
At lunch, Paati made dosas. Appa was coming home late from the tea factory. So Paati laid his hot dosas in a steel box lined with a cotton cloth. She folded the cloth over them and closed the lid.
'Arjun, watch,' said Meenakshi. 'The cloth is like your sweater. The dosas were hot when they went in, so the cloth will keep them hot.'
When Appa came home half an hour later, Paati opened the box. A little steam rose out. The dosas were still warm.
Arjun looked at the box, then at his sweater. 'So a sweater keeps hot things hot,' he said.
'And cold things cold,' said Meenakshi. She hugged her sweater around her. 'I'm the heater,' she said, 'and my sweater is the lid.'
story.epiphany: For the parent: Meenakshi notices that her sweater was cold on the chair and warm on her. Arjun's cold idli stayed cold inside a sweater, while hot dosas stayed warm inside a cloth. She works out that a sweater or a cloth makes no warmth. It keeps whatever warmth is already there, and the warmth in her sweater came from her own body.
ask: Meenakshi's sweater was cold on the chair. Why did it feel warm after two minutes?
Arjun wrapped his cold idli in his sweater. Why did it stay cold?
Meenakshi counted five things that make warmth. Can you name three of them?
Why did Appa's dosas stay warm in the cloth-lined box?
art: A girl at a frosty window in a hill house, with white frost on the grass outside and a red sweater folded on a chair.
A small boy with a bundle made from a blue sweater beside his plate, while a crow with puffed-up feathers watches from a wall.
A grandmother, a girl and a boy on a sunny verandah with tumblers of milk, and a cat stretched out in a patch of sunlight.
A steel box lined with a white cotton cloth, opened to show folded dosas with a little steam rising.

experiments.title: The Sweater and the Coconut Oil: does a sweater warm things up?
experiments.context: In this experiment you take two small katoris of coconut oil that have been in the fridge, so the oil is white and hard. You wrap one in a sweater and leave one bare. Then you watch which oil melts first.
experiments.question: If a sweater makes warmth, the oil inside it should melt first. Does it?
experiments.predict: Guess first. Which oil will melt first: the bare one, or the one wrapped in the sweater? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: Both katoris are the same, with the same amount of oil, and both come out of the fridge at the same time. They sit on the same table, out of the sun and away from the fan. Only the sweater is different. We check both at the same times.

materials.item: coconut oil, 1 big spoon for each katori
two small steel katoris that are the same
a woollen sweater or shawl. If you have no woollens, use a thick towel folded four times.
a clock or a phone timer

schedule.what: An hour before, put the oil in the fridge. Then wrap one katori, guess, and check both at 10, 20 and 30 minutes. Do the warmth hunt while you wait.

experiments.record: Draw the two katoris at each check. Colour the hard oil white and the runny oil yellow.

data.label: Bare katori
data.value: 10 minutes: clear at the edges. 20 minutes: mostly runny. 30 minutes: all runny.

data.label: Katori in the sweater
data.value: 10 minutes: all white. 20 minutes: all white. 30 minutes: a little clear at the edge.

setup.art: Two small steel katoris, each with a big spoon of coconut oil, sitting on a shelf inside a fridge.
setup.caption: 1. Put a big spoon of coconut oil in each katori. Leave them in the fridge for an hour.

setup.art: A girl wrapping one katori of white, hard coconut oil in a folded sweater, with the other katori bare beside it on a table.
setup.caption: 2. Wrap one katori in a sweater, under and over. Leave the other bare.

setup.art: The same table later: the bare katori with clear runny oil, and the sweater folded back to show white hard oil.
setup.caption: 3. Every 10 minutes, peep into both. Which oil is melting?

flow.do: 1. Take both katoris out of the fridge. 2. Let your child tilt them gently and look at the oil. 3. Hand them the sweater to hold.
flow.say: Look at the oil. It is white and hard, because the fridge made it cold. Now hold the sweater. We call sweaters warm clothes. What do you think a sweater does?
flow.kid: Look at the oil. It is white and hard. Now hold the sweater. What does a sweater do?

ask.q: What do you think a sweater does?
good: It makes you warm.
It keeps the warm in.
Any answer is fine here. The test will check it.

flow.parent: Coconut oil is white and hard when it is cooler than about 24 degrees, and a clear liquid when it is warmer. In a warm home the oil in the bottle is already runny, and an hour in the fridge makes it hard. If your room is cooler than about 24 degrees, the oil will not melt on the table. Then use two steel tumblers of the same warm tap water instead. Wrap one in the sweater, and feel which one is warmer after 30 minutes.

flow.do: Ask for a guess and a reason. Write the guess in the table.
flow.say: We will wrap one katori in the sweater and leave the other bare. Which oil will melt first? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Which oil will melt first, the bare one or the wrapped one? Why?

good: The wrapped one, because sweaters are warm.
The bare one, because the sweater keeps the cold in.

flow.parent: Most children guess the sweater one, because sweaters are 'warm'. Do not say what will happen.

flow.do: 1. Fold the sweater into a thick pad. 2. Put one katori on it and fold the sweater over the top, so it is covered all round. 3. Put the bare katori beside it. 4. Start the timer.
flow.say: Let's wrap this one all round, under and on top. The other one stays bare. Now we start the timer.
flow.kid: Wrap one katori all round in the sweater. Leave the other bare. Start the timer.
flow.parent: Keep both out of sunlight and away from the fan, so only the sweater is different.

flow.do: 1. At 10 minutes, open the sweater just enough to peep in, then close it. 2. Tilt each katori a little. Is there runny oil? 3. Draw both. 4. Do the same at 20 and 30 minutes.
flow.say: Time to peep. Tilt the bare katori. Is the oil runny? Now peep into the sweater, quickly. Is that oil runny?
flow.kid: Peep into both katoris. Tilt them gently. Which oil is runny?
flow.parent: While you wait between checks, do the warmth hunt (the Make It or Keep It activity). In a warm room, the bare oil usually turns clear at the edges within about 10 to 15 minutes. It is mostly runny by about 20 to 30 minutes. The wrapped oil stays white much longer. If it is still hard at 30 minutes, that is your answer: the sweater made it slower. You can look again later. In a cooler room, keep checking until the bare oil has melted.

flow.do: Put the two katoris side by side, both open. Ask what your child saw, and why. Then ask the check question.
flow.say: Which oil melted first? What did the sweater do to the cold oil? Did it warm it up, or keep it cold?
flow.kid: Which oil melted first? Did the sweater warm the oil, or keep it cold?

ask.q: Why did the bare oil melt first?
good: The room was warmer than the oil, and the room's warmth got in.
The sweater stopped the warmth getting in, so that oil stayed hard.

flow.parent: Wait for your child's own claim and reason first. Then say it plainly: the room's warmth was moving into both katoris. The sweater slowed it down. A sweater makes no warmth. It only slows heat moving in or out.

check.q: The oil in the sweater stayed hard for longer. What does that show?
options: The sweater slowed the room's warmth from getting in.
The sweater made the oil colder than the fridge.
The sweater made a lot of warmth.
check.why: If the sweater made warmth, the wrapped oil would have melted first. It kept the oil cold, so it was slowing warmth from getting in.

flow.do: Ask your child to put the same sweater on for two minutes, then feel inside it.
flow.say: Now put the sweater on. Wait two minutes. Does it feel warm now? The sweater makes no warmth. So where is this warmth coming from?
flow.kid: Put the sweater on. Wait two minutes. Is it warm? Where does the warmth come from?

ask.q: Where does the warmth come from?
good: From me.
From my body. The sweater keeps it in.

flow.think: If you wrapped a hot dosa in a cloth, what would the cloth do?

experiments.title: The Warm Spot Race: where does ice melt fastest?
experiments.context: In this experiment you put a small ice cube in each of four places. One cube sits in your own hand, and three sit on steel plates. Then you watch which ice cube melts first.
experiments.question: Which place melts ice fastest: your hand, a sunny spot, the table or the floor?
experiments.predict: Guess first. Which ice cube will melt first, and which last? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: The four ice cubes are the same size and come from the same tray. All four go to their places at the same moment. Only the place is different.
results_table: Minutes until no ice is left

materials.item: four small ice cubes of the same size from the freezer tray, kept in the freezer until you start
four small steel plates or katoris that are the same
a clock or a phone timer

schedule.what: Put the four ice cubes in their places, and check every 2 minutes until all have melted.

experiments.record: Write 1, 2, 3 and 4 next to each place, in the order the ice cubes melted.

example_chart.title: Made-up example results
example_chart.y: Minutes until no ice is left

setup.art: Four small steel plates in a row, each with one small ice cube on it.
setup.caption: 1. Put four small ice cubes of the same size on four plates.

setup.art: One ice cube held in a child's closed hand over a plate, with the other plates on a sunny window sill, a table and a shady floor.
setup.caption: 2. Hold one cube in your hand over a plate. Put the other plates in three different places.

setup.art: A child opening their hand to show a small wet ice cube nearly gone, with water on the plate under it.
setup.caption: 3. Check every 2 minutes. Which ice cube melts first?

flow.do: 1. Choose four places with your child: your child's hand, a sunny spot, the table and the floor in the shade. 2. Take four ice cubes of the same size from the freezer tray, only when everyone is ready.
flow.say: We will race four ice cubes. One will sit in your hand. Which one will melt first? Which last? Why?
flow.kid: Which ice cube will melt first? Which will melt last? Why?

good: My hand, because I am warm.
The sunny spot, because the Sun is hot.

flow.parent: Keep the tray in the freezer until you start. If no sunlight comes into your home, use a spot next to a warm machine instead, such as a television or a wifi box that has been on for a while.

flow.do: 1. Put the cubes in their places at the same time. 2. Your child holds one cube in a closed hand, over a plate. 3. Every 2 minutes, look at all four. 4. Write the order they melt in.
flow.say: Hold the ice cube in your closed hand, over the plate. Every 2 minutes we look at all four. Which one has melted?
flow.kid: Hold the ice in your hand. Every 2 minutes, check all four. Which is gone?
flow.parent: The cube in the hand, or the one in strong sun, usually melts first, in a few minutes. The table and the floor are slower, and they may melt at nearly the same time. If so, give them the same number. If the hand gets too cold, swap hands. Stop at 20 minutes and compare how much ice is left on each plate.

flow.do: Talk about the order together. Ask what your child found, and why.
flow.say: Which ice cube melted first? Which melted last? What does the cube in your hand tell you about your hand?
flow.kid: Which ice melted first? What does that tell you about your hand?

ask.q: Why did the ice in your hand melt so fast?
good: My hand is warmer than the room.
My body makes warmth, and it went into the spoon.

check.q: Why does ice melt faster in your hand than on the table?
options: Your body makes warmth, so your hand is warmer than the table.
Your hand is colder than the table.
The table makes the oil hard.
check.why: Your body makes warmth from food. Your hand is warmer than the room, so heat moves from your hand into the ice faster.

activities.title: Make It or Keep It? A warmth hunt at home
activities.context: In this activity you walk round your home and find warm things. For each one, you decide: does it make warmth, or does it only keep warmth in?

materials.item: a sheet of paper with two columns: 'Makes warmth' and 'Keeps warmth in'

schedule.what: Find 6 or more warm things at home and sort them into the two columns.

activities.record: Draw each thing in its column. Count how many are in each column.

setup.art: A sheet of paper with two columns headed 'Makes warmth' and 'Keeps warmth in', with a small sun drawn in the first column and a folded blanket in the second.
setup.caption: 1. Make a two-column sheet.

setup.art: A girl looking at a quilt folded on a bed, then at a sunny window, with her sheet in her hand.
setup.caption: 2. Find a warm thing. Does it make warmth or keep it in?

flow.do: Show the two columns. Do one example together: a quilt.
flow.say: Some things make warmth. Some things only keep warmth in. A quilt on the bed. Is it warm by itself, or does it keep your warmth in?
flow.kid: Look at a quilt. Does it make warmth, or keep it in?

good: No, it keeps my warmth in.
It is only warm when I am under it.

flow.do: 1. Walk round the home together. 2. Find at least 6 warm things or things that keep warmth in. 3. Your child draws each one in a column.
flow.say: Let's hunt. Look in the kitchen, the bedroom and at the windows. What makes warmth? What keeps warmth in?
flow.kid: Hunt for warm things. Draw each one in a column.
flow.parent: Good finds: sunlight at a window, the gas stove (look, don't touch), an iron box, a kettle, a pet, a family member. Keepers: a quilt, a sweater, a cap, socks, a pot lid, a cloth over chapatis, a flask. Never touch the stove or a hot iron.

flow.do: Count each column together. Ask the check question.
flow.say: How many things make warmth? How many keep it in? Is there anything you are not sure about?
flow.kid: Count each column. Which column has more?

check.q: Which one makes its own warmth?
options: A dog asleep on the mat
A woollen cap
A folded blanket
check.why: A dog's body makes warmth from food. A cap and a blanket only keep warmth in.

activities.title: Haa and Whoo: warm breath, cool breath
activities.context: In this activity you breathe on your hand in two ways. Your breath feels warm one way and cool the other way.

materials.item: your own hand and your own breath

schedule.what: Breathe 'haa' and blow 'whoo' on your hand, and talk about the difference.

activities.record: Draw your mouth open wide for haa and small and round for whoo. Write warm or cool under each.

setup.art: A child holding a palm close to a wide-open mouth, breathing out softly, with a soft orange cloud.
setup.caption: 1. Open your mouth wide. Breathe out softly on your palm: haa.

setup.art: The same child with lips small and round, blowing on the palm, with blue lines.
setup.caption: 2. Make your lips small and round. Blow hard: whoo.

flow.do: Show your child how to hold a palm near their mouth and breathe out slowly with the mouth wide open, saying 'haa'.
flow.say: Hold your palm near your mouth. Open wide and breathe out slowly: haa. How does it feel?
flow.kid: Open your mouth wide. Breathe 'haa' on your palm. Warm or cool?

good: Warm.
Warm and a bit wet.

flow.do: Now ask your child to make their lips small and round, and blow hard on the same palm.
flow.say: Now make your lips small and round. Blow hard: whoo. Is it the same breath? Why does it feel different?
flow.kid: Make your lips small. Blow 'whoo'. Warm or cool now?

good: It comes out fast.
It feels like a fan.

flow.parent: Both breaths come from inside your warm body. Slow 'haa' breath reaches your hand still warm. Fast 'whoo' breath drags cooler room air along with it. Moving air also carries warmth off your skin, like a fan does.

flow.do: Ask the check question.
flow.say: So which way would you breathe to warm cold hands?
flow.kid: Which way warms cold hands: haa or whoo?

check.q: Which breath would warm your cold hands?
options: A slow 'haa' with your mouth wide open
A fast 'whoo' through small lips
Both are the same
check.why: Slow breath from a wide mouth reaches your hands still warm from your body. Fast breath pulls in cooler room air, and the moving air cools your skin.

activities.title: Where Is My Body Warmest? A touch map
activities.context: In this activity you touch the back of your hand to different parts of your body. You find the warm parts and the cooler parts, and mark them on a drawing of yourself.

materials.item: a sheet of paper. Draw a simple body outline on it: a round head, a body, two arms and two legs.
a red crayon and a blue crayon

schedule.what: Feel seven parts of your body and colour them red for warm and blue for cooler.

activities.record: Colour the body outline: red for the warmest parts, blue for the cooler parts.

setup.art: A child pressing the back of one hand gently against their neck.
setup.caption: 1. Touch the back of your hand to one part of your body.

setup.art: A body outline on paper with red on the neck and tummy, and blue on the nose, ears, fingers and toes.
setup.caption: 2. Colour warm parts red and cooler parts blue.

flow.do: Help your child touch the back of one hand to each part in turn. Try the forehead, neck, tummy (lift the shirt a little), nose, ears, fingers and feet.
flow.say: Touch the back of your hand to your neck. Warm or cool? Now your nose. Now your tummy. Now your toes.
flow.kid: Touch your neck. Warm or cool? Now your nose. Now your toes.
flow.parent: Most children find the neck and tummy warmest, and the nose, ears, fingers and toes cooler. These parts stick out, so they lose heat faster.

flow.do: Your child colours the outline.
flow.say: Colour the warm parts red and the cool parts blue. Which parts are cool? Do you see a pattern?
flow.kid: Colour warm parts red. Colour cool parts blue. Do you see a pattern?

good: My nose, ears, fingers and toes.
The parts that stick out.

flow.do: Ask the check question.
flow.say: On a cold morning, which parts would need a cap and socks?
flow.kid: Which parts need a cap and socks on a cold day?

check.q: Why do your toes feel cooler than your tummy?
options: Toes stick out and lose warmth faster.
Toes make more warmth than the tummy.
Toes have no blood.
check.why: Your warmth is made inside your body. Parts that stick out, like toes, fingers, ears and the nose, lose it faster to the air.

games.title: Makes It, Keeps It or Cools It? A sorting card game
games.players: 2 to 4 players, or a parent and a child.
games.context: This is a card game. Each card shows something from daily life. Players decide: does it make warmth, keep warmth in, or cool you down?

items.f: The Sun shining through a window
A gas flame under the dosa tawa
A lit diya (oil lamp) on Karthigai Deepam
An iron box switched on
An electric kettle boiling water
Rubbing your hands together fast
Your own body, all day and night
A hen sitting on her eggs
A woollen sweater
A quilt on the bed
A woollen cap
A cotton cloth around hot chapatis
A lid on a pot of rasam
A flask of hot tea
A pair of socks
A crow's fluffed-up feathers
A ceiling fan blowing on you
The shade of a neem tree
A wet cloth on your forehead
A cool bath on a hot day
Sitting on a cool stone floor
Sucking on an ice lolly
Running up and down the stairs
A buffalo lying in a pond on a hot day

rules: Put the three pile labels in a row on the floor.
Mix the 24 cards and make a stack with the words side up. The answer is on the other side.
On your turn, take the top card and read it out loud. Do not turn it over yet.
Put it next to the label you think is right, and say why.
Now turn the card over to check. If you were right, keep the card. If not, put it at the bottom of the stack.
When the stack is empty, the player with the most cards wins. If two players have the same number, they both win.

setup.art: Three paper labels on a floor: 'Makes warmth' with a sun, 'Keeps warmth in' with a sweater, 'Cools you down' with a fan.
setup.caption: 1. Lay out the three labels.

setup.art: A girl holding a card that says 'A woollen cap', about to put it next to the 'Keeps warmth in' label, while her grandfather watches.
setup.caption: 2. Read a card. Put it by a label and say why.

flow.do: Lay out the labels and read the rules together.
flow.say: Each card is something from daily life. You decide: does it make warmth, keep warmth in, or cool you down? Then turn it over to check.
flow.kid: Read your card. Does it make warmth, keep warmth in, or cool you down?

flow.do: Play. After each card, ask the player for their reason.
flow.say: A woollen cap. Does a cap make warmth? Where does the warmth under a cap come from?
flow.kid: Why did you put it there? Say your reason.

ask.q: Where does the warmth under a cap come from?
good: From my head. The cap keeps it in.
From my body.

flow.parent: The hen card is 'makes warmth', because her body makes it. Her feathers keep it in. If a child says both, that is a very good answer: give them the card.

flow.do: Ask the check question.
flow.say: One last tricky one.
flow.kid: Answer one last tricky card.

check.q: A cat sleeps in a sunny spot. Which thing there makes warmth?
options: The Sun and the cat's own body
Only the floor
Nothing makes warmth
check.why: The Sun's light warms the cat, and the cat's body makes warmth from food. The floor only gets warm from the sunlight.

projects.title: My Book of Warm Things: two days
projects.context: In this project you make a small book. Six pages each show one thing that warms you up, and say whether it makes warmth or keeps it in. The last page is about you.

materials.item: 3 sheets of paper, folded in half and stapled or tied with thread

schedule.what: Make the book. Draw three things that make warmth: one from the sky, one from the kitchen, and one living body.
Draw three things that keep warmth in. On the last page, draw yourself and write 'I make my own warmth'.

projects.record: A book with seven pages. Six pages have 'makes' or 'keeps' written on them, and the last page is you.

setup.art: Three sheets of paper folded together and tied with a thread to make a small book, with 'My Warm Things' on the cover.
setup.caption: 1. Fold three sheets and tie them into a book.

setup.art: An open page with a drawing of a hen sitting on eggs and the word 'makes' written under it.
setup.caption: 2. Draw one warm thing on each page. Write makes or keeps.

flow.do: Day 1: help your child make the book and draw three things that make warmth.
flow.say: Draw three things that make warmth. One from the sky, one from the kitchen, and one living body. Write 'makes' under each.
flow.kid: Draw three things that make warmth. Write 'makes' under each.

ask.q: Which living body did you draw?
good: Me.
Our dog.
A hen keeping her eggs warm.

flow.do: Day 2: help your child draw three things that keep warmth in, and a last page of themselves.
flow.say: Now draw three things that keep warmth in. Write 'keeps' under each. On the last page, draw yourself. Who makes your warmth?
flow.kid: Draw three things that keep warmth in. Then draw yourself.

ask.q: Who makes the warmth inside your sweater?
good: I do.
My body, from my food.

challenges.title: Keep a Dosa Warm for 20 Minutes
challenges.context: This is a design challenge. Someone at home will eat in 20 minutes. Can you keep a hot dosa or chapati warm for them, using only things from home?
challenges.problem: Someone at home will eat in 20 minutes. Keep one hot dosa or chapati warm, without putting it back on the stove.
constraints: No stove, oven or electricity after the dosa is made.
Leave a second dosa bare on a plate, so you can compare.
materials: two hot dosas or chapatis, made by a grown-up
clean cotton cloths or kitchen towels
a steel dabba with a lid
challenges.safety: A grown-up makes the dosas and hands them over. A dosa straight from the tawa can burn fingers, so wait until it is safe to hold.
general: Wrap the dosa in a clean cotton cloth, the way many families wrap chapatis.
Put it in a steel dabba and close the lid.
Use a hot case (an insulated box for rotis), if your home has one.
creative: Put the dosa in a dabba, then wrap the whole dabba in a towel.
Stack it between other hot dosas, so they keep each other warm.
Rinse the dabba with warm water first, so the steel is not cold.
challenges.your_turn: Make your own dosa keeper. After 20 minutes, touch both dosas. Is yours warmer than the bare one? Draw your design.

setup.art: Two dosas on a counter: one on a bare plate, and one being wrapped in a cotton cloth by a girl.
setup.caption: 1. Wrap one hot dosa. Leave one bare on a plate.

setup.art: The same girl 20 minutes later, touching the bare dosa with one hand and the wrapped dosa with the other.
setup.caption: 2. After 20 minutes, touch both. Which is warmer?

flow.do: Read the problem. Ask for ideas before showing any.
flow.say: Someone will eat in 20 minutes. How can we keep this dosa warm without the stove?
flow.kid: How can you keep a dosa warm for 20 minutes?

good: A cloth.
A box with a lid.
My sweater, but a clean cloth is better for food.

flow.do: 1. The grown-up makes two dosas. 2. Your child wraps one with their design. 3. The other goes on a bare plate.
flow.say: Wrap one dosa your way. Put the other on a plate, with nothing over it. Start the timer.
flow.kid: Wrap one dosa. Leave one bare. Start the timer.

flow.do: Wait 20 minutes. Do another activity meanwhile. Then touch both dosas.
flow.say: Touch the bare dosa. Now touch yours. Which is warmer? Why?
flow.kid: Touch both dosas. Which is warmer? Why?

ask.q: Why did your dosa stay warmer?
good: The cloth kept its heat in.
The heat could not get out fast.

flow.do: Ask the check question.
flow.say: Did your wrapping make warmth, or keep it in?
flow.kid: Did your wrapping make warmth, or keep it in?

check.q: Why did the wrapped dosa stay warm?
options: The cloth slowed its heat from leaving.
The cloth made new heat.
The bare dosa got hotter.
check.why: The dosa was hot when it went in. The cloth made no warmth, but it slowed the heat from leaving.

challenges.title: Warm Your Cold Hands, No Fire Allowed
challenges.context: This is a challenge. First your hands get cold from holding a tumbler of fridge water. Then you find the fastest way to warm them, with no stove, no heater and no hot water.
challenges.problem: After holding a cold tumbler, your hands are cold. Find ways to warm them up in one minute, without fire, a heater or hot water.
constraints: No stove, heater, hot water or hair dryer.
Try each idea for one minute.
Cool your hands on the cold tumbler again before each new idea.
materials: a steel tumbler of cold water from the fridge
general: Tuck your hands under your arms.
Sit on your hands for a minute.
creative: Jump up and down for a minute, then feel your hands.
Ask someone at home to hold your hands in theirs.
Pull socks over your hands like gloves.
challenges.your_turn: Which idea warmed your hands best? Did any idea make warmth, and which only kept it in? Draw your best idea.

setup.art: A child holding a frosty steel tumbler of cold water in both hands.
setup.caption: 1. Hold the cold tumbler for 30 seconds.

setup.art: The same child with hands tucked under their arms, smiling.
setup.caption: 2. Try one idea for one minute. Are your hands warm again?

flow.do: Your child holds the cold tumbler in both hands for 30 seconds.
flow.say: Hold this cold tumbler for 30 seconds. How do your hands feel? Where did their warmth go?
flow.kid: Hold the cold tumbler. How do your hands feel now?

good: Into the cold tumbler.
Into the water.

flow.do: Try three ideas, one minute each. Cool the hands on the tumbler again before each one.
flow.say: Try your first idea for one minute. Then cool your hands again, and try the next one. Which works best?
flow.kid: Try one idea for a minute. Then try the next.
flow.parent: Rubbing, jumping and the armpits work well. Rubbing makes warmth by friction. Jumping makes your muscles make more warmth. Armpits, socks and sitting on your hands keep your body's warmth close to your hands.

flow.do: Talk about which ideas made warmth and which kept it in. Ask the check question.
flow.say: Which ideas made new warmth? Which ones only kept your warmth in?
flow.kid: Which ideas made warmth? Which only kept it in?

check.q: Pulling socks over your hands warms them. Why?
options: The socks keep your body's warmth in.
The socks make heat.
The socks are hot from the cupboard.
check.why: Socks make no warmth. Your hands make warmth from your body, and the socks slow it from escaping.

worksheets.title: Makes warmth or keeps it in (core)

items.p: A grown-up reads each one. Does it make warmth, or keep warmth in? Sort them.
items.why: The Sun, a flame and a living body make warmth. A quilt, a cap and a lid only slow warmth from leaving. A strong answer can say why for each.

items.p: Draw a line from each warm thing to what made it warm.
items.why: Each warm thing got its warmth from something that makes warmth: sunlight, a flame, rubbing or a living body.
items.art: Four pictures on the left (a window sill, a tawa, two palms, eggs under a hen) and four on the right (the Sun, a flame, rubbing hands, a hen).

items.p: In the Sweater and Coconut Oil test, which oil stayed white and hard for longer?
opts: The oil wrapped in the sweater
Both melted at the same time
items.why: The sweater slowed the room's warmth from getting in, so the wrapped oil stayed cold and hard for longer.
items.context: This question is about the Sweater and Coconut Oil test. You took two katoris of cold, hard coconut oil out of the fridge, wrapped one in a sweater and left one bare.

items.p: An ice cube melts fast in your hand because your hand is warmer than the ice.
items.why: True. Your body makes warmth, so your hand is warmer than the ice. Heat moves from your hand into the ice.

items.p: Draw one thing in your home that makes warmth, and one thing that keeps warmth in.
items.a: For example, the Sun at the window, and a quilt on the bed.
items.why: A strong drawing shows one maker of warmth, like the Sun, a flame or a body, and one keeper, like a quilt, a cap or a lid.

items.p: When you are cold, your muscles shake without you meaning to. This is called to ______.
items.why: Shivering makes warmth. Your muscles shake and give out heat.

items.p: Say out loud, and a grown-up writes it down: why does your sweater feel warm when you wear it?
items.a: Because my body makes warmth, and the sweater keeps it close to me.
items.why: A strong answer says the warmth comes from the body, and the sweater only keeps it in.

items.p: Kavya, a girl in Class 2, found 3 things that make warmth and 4 things that keep warmth in. How many things did she find?
items.why: 3 and 4 more make 7.

items.p: Arjun, a boy aged 5, and his sister Meenakshi, aged 8, talk about the coconut oil test before they try it.

views.says: A sweater is warm, so it will melt the oil fast.
A sweater only keeps warmth where it is. The oil is cold, so it will stay cold.

items.ask: Who do you agree with? Use what you saw in the test. Then say one thing the other person has right.
items.a: Meenakshi. The wrapped oil stayed hard longer, so the sweater kept the cold oil cold. Arjun is right that we feel warm in a sweater, but that warmth comes from our body.
items.why: A strong answer uses the test result as evidence, and is fair to Arjun's idea.

items.p: Why do your hands get warm when you rub them together?
opts: Rubbing takes warmth from the air.
Your hands were hot inside all along.
items.why: Rubbing makes warmth. That is one way things get warm, along with the Sun, fire, electricity and living bodies.

items.p: Why did the bare coconut oil melt first?
opts: The room was warmer than the oil, and the room's heat moved into it.
The oil in the sweater was a different oil.
items.why: The oil came from the cold fridge, so the room was warmer. Heat moves from warmer to cooler things, and nothing slowed it down for the bare oil.

items.p: Put these in order, from the hottest to the coldest.
items.why: Hot tea is much hotter than a hand. A hand is warmer than fridge water. Ice is the coldest.

items.p: Label the body outline: warm, or cooler? Use what you felt in the touch map.
items.why: The middle of the body is warmest. Parts that stick out, like the nose and toes, lose warmth faster.
items.art: An outline of a child with four empty label lines, pointing to the neck, tummy, nose and toes.

items.p: A puppy sleeping in a heap with other puppies stays warmer than a puppy sleeping alone. Why? You can say it and a grown-up can write it down.
items.a: Every puppy's body makes warmth. In a heap, less of each puppy is out in the cold air, so less warmth escapes. They also warm each other.
items.why: A strong answer says the warmth comes from the puppies' bodies, and the heap keeps more of it in.

items.p: Three of these make warmth. Which one only keeps warmth in?
items.why: A quilt makes no warmth. The Sun, a flame and a hen's body all make warmth.

items.p: You lose most of your body heat through your head, so a cap matters most.
items.why: False. A bare head loses about as much heat as any other bare part of the same size. It seems like more only because the rest of you is covered.

items.p: On a cold morning, a sparrow or a crow puffs up their feathers. Draw how they look, and say why they do it.
items.a: A round, fluffy bird. The puffed feathers hold more still air, which keeps their warmth in.
items.why: A strong answer shows the fluffed shape and says the feathers keep the bird's own warmth in.

items.p: A ceiling fan cools you on a hot day. How?
opts: The moving air carries warmth away from your skin.
The fan blows out cold air it makes.
The fan makes the room colder than the fridge.
items.why: A fan makes no cold. It moves the air, and the moving air carries your warmth away and dries sweat.

items.p: It is a cold morning in Shillong. Kavya and her friend Divya want to get warm before school.

views.says: Put on a sweater. It keeps you warm all day.
Run and jump. Your body makes new warmth.

items.ask: Which idea do you think is better? Say why. Then say one good thing about the other idea.
items.a: Both help. Running makes new warmth fast, but you can't run all day. A sweater makes no warmth, but it keeps the warmth you make for hours. The best plan uses both.
items.why: A strong answer sees that one idea makes warmth and the other keeps it, and that both have a use.

items.p: A material that slows heat moving in or out is called an ______.
items.why: Wool, cloth and feathers are insulators. They slow heat moving through them.

items.p: Arjun, a boy aged 5, wrapped his cold idli in his sweater to warm it up. What will happen? What could he do instead? You can say it and a grown-up can write it down.
items.a: The idli will stay cold, because the sweater makes no warmth. He could ask a grown-up to warm it on the stove or in steam.
items.why: A strong answer says the sweater can only keep the warmth that is already there, and names a real maker of warmth.

items.p: Some people say mango heats the body and curd cools it. What have scientists found?
opts: They have not found that these foods change body temperature by much.
A mango raises body temperature by 5 degrees.
Curd is colder than ice, so it cools you.
items.why: Many families feel that foods heat or cool them. But scientists have not found that a mango or curd changes body temperature by much.

items.p: A hen sits on her eggs to keep them warm. Two girls argue about it.

views.says: The hen's feathers keep the eggs warm.
No, the hen's body makes the warmth.

items.ask: Who is right? Say why. Then say what the other girl has right.
items.a: Both are partly right. The hen's body makes the warmth from her food. Her feathers keep it in, around the eggs.
items.why: A strong answer separates making warmth from keeping it, and gives each girl her part.

items.p: You hold a cold steel tumbler of fridge water in your hands. Draw an arrow to show which way the heat moves.
items.a: An arrow from the hand into the tumbler.
items.why: Heat moves from warmer to cooler. Your hand is warmer, so heat moves from your hand into the cold tumbler. That is why your hands get cold.

items.p: After a swim you shiver. How does shivering help you? You can say it and a grown-up can write it down.
items.a: Shivering is your muscles shaking. Working muscles make warmth, so shivering makes warmth for your body.
items.why: A strong answer says shivering makes warmth, because muscles that work give out heat.

items.p: If you wrap a stone in a blanket all night, it becomes warmer than the room.
items.why: False. A blanket makes no warmth and a stone makes none. In the morning, the stone is as warm as the room.

items.p: A wet cloth on a hot forehead cools you by taking warmth away from your skin.
items.why: True. Heat moves from your warm skin into the cooler wet cloth, and the water carries warmth away as it dries.

items.p: You forget a hot cup of filter coffee on the table. An hour later it is cool. Where did its heat go?
opts: Into the air and the table around it
items.why: Heat moves from a hotter thing into the cooler things around it. The coffee warmed the air and the table a tiny bit.

items.p: A friend says: 'A sweater kept the cold oil cold. So wear a sweater in summer to stay cool!' Is your friend right? Say why. You can say it and a grown-up can write it down.
items.a: No. Your body keeps making warmth, and a sweater would keep that warmth in. You would get hotter. The oil makes no warmth, so the sweater only kept its cold.
items.why: A strong answer remembers that the body makes its own warmth, while the oil does not.

items.p: Match each animal to how they keep warm.
pairs: A dog on a cold night
A crow on a cold morning
Held skin to skin on a parent's chest
items.why: Each one keeps the warmth their body makes: curling up, fluffing feathers, huddling and skin-to-skin care all slow heat from leaving.
items.art: Four small pictures: a curled-up dog, a fluffy crow, a huddle of penguins, and a parent holding a tiny baby against their chest.

quiz.p: Which word means how hot or cold something is?
quiz.why: Temperature tells how hot or cold something is. Weight tells how heavy, and colour is what we see.
A flame burns and makes warmth. Choosing the shawl or socks may mean thinking woollens make warmth. They only keep it in.

quiz.p: A sweater has been lying on a chair all night. How warm is it?
opts: As warm as the chair and the room
quiz.why: A sweater makes no warmth, so it is as warm as the things around it.

quiz.p: Where does the warmth inside your sweater come from?
quiz.why: Your body makes warmth from food. The wool only keeps it close to you.

quiz.p: Usha, a girl in Class 2, tests a sweater on cold coconut oil. What should be the same for both katoris?
opts: The oil, the katori, the table and the time
Only the colour of the katoris
quiz.why: In a fair test, only one thing changes: here, the sweater. Everything else stays the same.

quiz.p: Usha wants her coconut oil test to be fair. Which change would make it unfair?
opts: Putting one katori in the sun and one in the shade
Using the same amount of oil in both
Starting the timer for both at the same time
quiz.why: In a fair test, only the sweater is different. Sun on one katori would change the test too, so we could not tell what melted the oil.

quiz.p: A hot idli sits on a plate for an hour. What happens?
opts: It cools down to the warmth of the room.
quiz.why: Hot things cool down until they are as warm as the room around them.

quiz.p: Why do your cheeks get warm after you run up the stairs?
quiz.why: When muscles work hard, they make more warmth. The stairs make none.

quiz.p: On a cold night, how does a dog keep warm?
opts: They curl up into a ball.
They sit by an open window.
quiz.why: Curling up hides the parts that lose warmth fastest, so the dog's own warmth stays in.

quiz.p: On a hot day in Chennai, which helps you cool down?
opts: Sitting in the shade under a fan
quiz.why: Shade keeps the Sun's light off you, and the fan's moving air carries your warmth away. A quilt would keep your warmth in.

videos.title: Kangaroo mother care: keeping a small baby warm skin to skin
videos.why: Shows a mother or father holding a small baby against their bare chest, so the parent's body heat keeps the baby warm.
videos.check: Found by search: "Maternal health: Ensuring kangaroo mother care for every small or preterm baby" by World Health Organization (WHO), 3 minutes. A parent may preview it.

videos.title: How does huddling help penguins stay warm?
videos.why: Shows thousands of penguins standing close together, keeping in the warmth their bodies make.
videos.check: Found by search: "How Does Huddling Help Penguins Stay Warm?" by BBC Earth, 3 minutes. A parent may preview it.

videos.title: Why do woollen clothes keep us warm?
videos.why: Explains that wool traps still air and slows body heat from escaping, and that clothes make no heat themselves.
videos.check: Found by search: "Why do woolen clothes keep us warm?" by It's AumSum Time, 1 minute. A parent may preview it.

applications: Families keep chapatis and dosas warm in a cloth or a hot case, which slows their heat from escaping.
A flask keeps tea hot for hours, and keeps cold water cold, because it slows heat moving in or out.
Hospitals keep very small babies warm skin to skin on a parent's chest. This is called kangaroo mother care.
Soldiers on the cold mountains of Ladakh and Siachen wear many layers, because each layer keeps more body heat in.
Ice-cream sellers keep their boxes thickly lined, so the ice cream stays frozen in the hot sun.
In 1948, Mária Telkes, a scientist from Hungary working in America, built the heating for a house warmed by stored sunshine. The house was designed by the architect Eleanor Raymond.

spotted.text: In winter in Kashmir, people wear a long woollen cloak called a pheran, and some carry a small clay pot of hot coals, called a kangri, under it.
spotted.art: A person in a long woollen pheran in the snow, with the shape of a small basket pot under the cloak.

spotted.text: In Kerala and Tamil Nadu, cooked rice and curry are often kept warm in a heavy pot with its lid on.
spotted.art: A heavy pot with a lid on a kitchen counter, with a little steam escaping at the edge.

open_questions.q: Why is the inside of the human body about 37 degrees, and not cooler or warmer?
open_questions.why_open: Nobody knows for sure. One idea, from the scientist Arturo Casadevall and others, is that this warmth keeps most kinds of fungus from growing inside us, while not costing too much food.

open_questions.q: How does a plant feel a long winter, and remember the cold?
open_questions.why_open: Some plants flower only after a long cold spell. Caroline Dean and other scientists have found that cold slowly switches off a flowering brake in their cells, and the plant remembers this for months. Exactly how the cold is sensed is still being worked out.

open_questions.q: How much warmth do grown-ups make from special 'brown fat'?
open_questions.why_open: Babies have brown fat that makes warmth. Scientists found in 2009 that many grown-ups have some too. How much it matters for keeping a grown-up warm is still being studied.

maths.problem: In the coconut oil test, Lakshmi, a girl in Class 2, checked every 10 minutes. The bare oil was all runny at the 2nd check. The wrapped oil was all runny at the 5th check. How many minutes is that for each?
maths.answer: 20 minutes for the bare oil and 50 minutes for the wrapped oil.
maths.explain: Count in tens. 2 checks is 10, 20, so 20 minutes. 5 checks is 10, 20, 30, 40, 50, so 50 minutes.
maths.context: This is about the Sweater and Coconut Oil test, where you wrapped one katori of cold oil in a sweater and left one bare.
maths.why_maths: Counting in equal steps of 10 turns the number of checks into minutes, so we can compare the two katoris.

maths.problem: In the Warm Spot Race, the ice cube in the hand of Farhan, a boy in Class 2, melted at 4 minutes. The ice cube on the floor melted at 14 minutes. How many minutes longer did the floor ice take?
maths.explain: Count on from 4 to 14. That is 10. So the floor ice took 10 more minutes.
maths.context: This is about the Warm Spot Race, where you put ice cubes in different places.
maths.why_maths: Taking the smaller time from the bigger one shows how much faster your warm hand was than the floor.

maths.problem: In the warmth hunt, Nila, a girl in Class 2, made a tally: Makes warmth: |||| . Keeps warmth in: |||| | . Which column has more, and by how many?
maths.answer: Keeps warmth in has more, by 1. It has 6 and Makes warmth has 5.
maths.explain: Count the tally marks. The first column has 5 and the second has 6. 6 is 1 more than 5.
maths.context: This is about the warmth hunt, where you sorted warm things into 'Makes warmth' and 'Keeps warmth in'.
maths.why_maths: A tally lets you count each group quickly and compare them.

maths.problem: Divya, a girl in Class 2, says: 'The bare oil melted in 20 minutes. So the oil in the sweater will melt in 20 minutes too.' Will it? What would you expect instead?
maths.answer: No. It will take longer than 20 minutes, because the sweater slows the room's warmth getting in.
maths.explain: The sweater changes how fast warmth reaches the oil. So the times will not be the same. We expect a bigger number for the wrapped oil.
maths.context: This is about the Sweater and Coconut Oil test.
maths.why_maths: Predicting which number will be bigger helps us check our idea about what the sweater does.

roots.context: We have hunted for warm things, wrapped cold coconut oil in a sweater and felt our own warmth. Now we ask what the sweater test tells us about ourselves and the world.

deep_truth.truth: Your sweater kept the cold coconut oil hard, while the bare oil melted. So the sweater made no warmth. It only slowed the room's warmth getting in. When you wear it, the warmth you feel is your own body's.
deep_truth.habit: We call sweaters, shawls and quilts 'warm', as if warmth were stored in them. The coconut oil test shows a sweater keeps a cold thing cold just as well. It only slows heat moving in or out.
deep_truth.evidence: In the Sweater and Coconut Oil test, the bare oil melted first, and the oil inside the sweater stayed white and hard for longer. The same sweater, put on, felt warm within two minutes. In the Warm Spot Race, ice melted fastest in your own hand.

three.who_am_i: You are a warm body. Your cells make warmth from food all day and night, even while you sleep.
three.what_is_life: Living bodies make warmth and keep it. A hen warms her eggs with her body, and a dog curls up to keep their warmth in.
three.what_is_this_world: The world is full of warmth on the move: from the Sun, from fire and from bodies into the cooler things around them.

roots.thread: The Sun, a diya flame and your body look like very different things. Each of them is giving out energy as warmth. Your warmth came from your food, and your food got its energy from sunlight that a plant caught. So the warmth inside your sweater began as sunshine on a rice field. A sweater, a nest or a parent's arms keep that warmth near.

teachings.teaching: Bhrigu asked his father Varuna what the world comes from. After thinking hard, he understood: from food, living beings are born, by food they live.
teachings.link: Your body heat is made from food. Without food, a body has nothing to make warmth from.

teachings.teaching: Krishna says he is the fire inside the bodies of living beings, which digests their food, joined with the breath going in and out.
teachings.link: Long ago, people called the body's warmth a fire inside. Science agrees that your cells slowly use food with the air you breathe, and this gives out warmth.

science.text: Your cells use food and oxygen to get energy, and much of that energy comes out as warmth. This is why a living body stays warm.
Why animals like us keep our insides at about 37 degrees is not known for sure. One idea is that it keeps most fungi from growing in us.

other_view.view: Shivering and goosebumps are reflexes, switched on by nerves and one part of the brain, like a switch on a heater. They say the cells in your skin only send signals, and only the brain feels warm or cold.

practice.title: Feel your own warmth
practice.say: Sit still and shut your eyes. Cup your hands in front of your face, without touching it. Breathe out slowly through your mouth. Feel your breath warm your hands. Now rest both hands on your tummy. Feel the warmth there. You made that warmth yourself, from your breakfast. Where was it before it was in your breakfast?
practice.kid: Sit still. Shut your eyes. Cup your hands near your face. Breathe out slowly. Feel the warm breath. Now put your hands on your tummy. Feel the warmth. You made it from your food.

how_we_found_out.who: Edgar Rey Sanabria, a doctor in Bogotá, Colombia. Later, Sarmila Mazumder, Nita Bhandari and their team in India
how_we_found_out.story: For a long time, hospitals kept very small babies warm in incubators. An incubator is a warm box with a clear lid. Many doctors thought a very small baby needed one to stay warm. In 1978, a big hospital in Bogotá, the capital of Colombia, was crowded and had too few incubators. A doctor there, Edgar Rey Sanabria, tried something new. Mothers held their small babies upright against their bare chest, skin to skin, under their clothes, for many hours each day. The mother's body made the warmth, and her clothes kept it around the baby. A mother kangaroo carries her baby in a pouch, so people called this care kangaroo mother care. Many studies tested it after that. In Haryana, in India, a team led by Sarmila Mazumder and Nita Bhandari helped families do it at home. In 2019, they reported that more of the small babies survived. Today the World Health Organization advises it for small babies everywhere, and fathers can do it too.
how_we_found_out.wrong_idea: Many doctors thought a very small baby could only be kept warm safely in an incubator. Skin-to-skin care showed that a parent's own body heat can keep the baby warm.

founder: ideas/by_topic/energy.md, Heat Flow and Heat transfer: 'wrap bottles with different materials to test insulation' became the Sweater and Coconut Oil test (e1), changed to coconut oil so a child of 7 can see the result without a thermometer. 'Yoga poses to generate warmth' and 'meditate on inner warmth' became the roots practice. 'Game of matching objects to hot/cold categories' became the Makes It, Keeps It or Cools It card game (g1). 'Rub hands to feel warmth' is one idea in the cold hands challenge (c2).

Level 3 (sci.energy.heat.L3) has the two-hands bowl, the hot and cold tumbler test with a thermometer, the straw thermometer and the temperature diary, so this unit uses no thermometer and none of those activities. It leads on to Level 3 by noticing that hot things cool and cold things warm up.

playtest: Walked through every part as a parent and a child in a city flat. The coconut oil test needs only a fridge, two katoris and a sweater, and its time is now 45 minutes with checks at 10, 20 and 30 minutes, with a note for a cool room. Fixed the card game rules (the words side is up, ties win), the body-outline sheet, the book project page count, and the dosa and cold-hands challenges (no made-up names or assumed family). Fixed Arjun's age and the story's count of warm things, replaced repeated questions in the worksheets and quiz, introduced every made-up child, and cut the weakest joke.
